title: Adaptive chunking helpers for cross-SDK embeddings + rerank
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: Customers frequently build workflows that need to compute embeddings or rerank large result sets across multiple SDKs. Current SDK helpers either force a strict cursor-based pagination model or expose low-level batch primitives that don't account for variable per-item cost, streaming backpressure, or prefix/KV-cache affinities. This leads to duplicated app code, higher memory spikes, and user confusion when migrating between Python/TS/Go.

Goal: Ship a set of cross-language helper primitives that implement adaptive chunking (chunk size grows/shrinks based on observed latency and token cost), optional cursor compatibility, and a streaming-friendly API that supports backpressure and incremental yields. The helpers should: (1) make embeddings and rerank calls ergonomic in idiomatic Python/TS/Go; (2) default to safe memory usage for large inputs; (3) include retry/backoff and transparent batching to reduce per-item cost; (4) preserve deterministic ordering for rerank responses when required.

Design summary: We will implement a small surface in each SDK: a Chunker (manages adaptive chunk sizes), a StreamAdapter (yields results incrementally, supports pause/resume), and a CursorCompat shim (optional: emits cursors for customers who need server-side pagination). The Chunker samples latency/throughput and applies a capped exponential increase when the median latency remains below a target SLO. On latency spikes, it halves chunk size and signals the StreamAdapter to flush. Retries use the SDK unified retry policy with per-request idempotency hints.

Acceptance criteria:
- Python/TS/Go SDKs ship API parity for the helpers (same semantic behavior, idiomatic names).
- End-to-end examples exist for embeddings and rerank flows that handle 100k items with bounded memory (<250MB resident) in our CI smoke tests.
- Bench harness (small CI job) demonstrates at least 20% token-cost reduction vs naive per-item requests for typical PLG datasets.
- Docs + code samples published in the SDK repo and referenced in the Console quickstarts.

Trade-offs considered:
- Full cursor-first design would simplify server interaction but increase client complexity for streaming; we choose a hybrid defaults-to-streaming approach to optimize UX for large-batch inferencing.
- Adaptive heuristics increase client complexity and metrics surface area; mitigated by default conservative caps and opt-out flags.

Non-goals: Not implementing server-side batching or reordering heuristics; we rely on existing runtime routing and KV caching on the server side.

Notes: this ticket covers the helper design, cross-SDK API, and examples. Separate follow-ups will add telemetry dashboards and a dedicated SDK-configurable autoscaler plugin for Dedicated.

example_snippets:
Python example:
from redwood import SDKClient
from redwood.sdk.helpers import AdaptiveChunker, StreamAdapter
client = SDKClient()
chunker = AdaptiveChunker(target_latency_ms=120, max_chunk=256)
stream = StreamAdapter(client.embeddings.batch, chunker)
for result in stream.process(items):
    # results arrive incrementally, preserved order by default
    handle(result)
